# Anti-Patterns Catalogue

Every pattern below is **forbidden** in generated tests. When reviewing or
generating, treat any occurrence as a defect to fix.

---

## AP-01: Hollow `assertNotNull`

```java
// BAD
assertNotNull(result);
assertNotNull(result.getName());

// GOOD — assert the actual value
assertEquals("John", result.getName());
assertThat(result.getItems()).hasSize(3);
```

**Why forbidden:** `assertNotNull` passes for *any* non-null value. It proves the
code returned *something*, not the *right* thing. A bug that returns the wrong
value will not be caught.

**Fix:** Replace with `assertEquals`, `assertThat(...).contains(...)`, or another
value-level assertion. If the value is dynamic (e.g., UUID), assert the format
or length instead.

---

## AP-02: Tautological `assertTrue` / `assertFalse`

```java
// BAD
assertTrue(result instanceof OrderResponse);
assertTrue(list.size() > 0);
assertFalse(result == null);

// GOOD
assertInstanceOf(OrderResponse.class, result);
assertThat(list).isNotEmpty();
assertEquals("ORD-001", ((OrderResponse) result).getOrderId());
```

**Why forbidden:** These test structural properties, not business correctness.
`assertTrue(x instanceof T)` is also a weaker form of `assertInstanceOf` and
gives worse failure messages.

---

## AP-03: Try-Catch Exception Swallowing

```java
// BAD
@Test
void testInvalidInput() {
    try {
        service.process(null);
        fail("should throw");
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
        assertEquals("input required", e.getMessage());
    }
}

// GOOD
@Test
void process_nullInput_throwsIllegalArgument() {
    var ex = assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
        () -> service.process(null));
    assertEquals("input required", ex.getMessage());
}
```

**Why forbidden:** The try-catch pattern has three problems:
1. If an *unexpected* exception is thrown, the `catch` may miss it silently
2. If the code *doesn't* throw, the `fail()` call is easy to forget
3. It conflates the "should it throw?" question with "what did it throw?"

**Fix:** One `@Test` per error scenario using `assertThrows`. Assert the
exception message or properties on the returned exception object.

---

## AP-04: Redundant Tests

```java
// BAD — three tests that all exercise the same happy-path mapping
@Test void mapUser_setsFirstName() { assertEquals("John", dto.getFirstName()); }
@Test void mapUser_setsLastName()  { assertEquals("Doe",  dto.getLastName()); }
@Test void mapUser_setsEmail()     { assertEquals("j@d",  dto.getEmail()); }

// GOOD — one test that fully asserts the mapping
@Test
void mapUser_allFieldsMappedCorrectly() {
    var dto = mapper.toDto(user);
    assertEquals("John", dto.getFirstName());
    assertEquals("Doe",  dto.getLastName());
    assertEquals("j@d",  dto.getEmail());
}
```

**Why forbidden:** Each test has setup/teardown cost. Splitting single-object
mapping assertions into separate methods creates noise without increasing
confidence. Group assertions on the *same* logical object together.

**Exception:** If fields have *independent* mapping logic (e.g., one involves a
calculation, another involves a lookup), separate tests are appropriate.

---

## AP-05: Testing POJOs / Entities / DTOs

```java
// BAD — testing getter/setter auto-generated by Lombok or record accessors
@Test void testGetName() { user.setName("x"); assertEquals("x", user.getName()); }

// BAD — testing record construction
@Test void testRecord() { var r = new Foo("a"); assertEquals("a", r.name()); }
```

**Why forbidden:** These test language features (Java records, Lombok), not
business logic. Zero bugs are caught. Skip entirely.

**Exception:** If a POJO has *computed* methods (e.g., `getFullName()` that
concatenates first+last), test *that* method only.

---

## AP-06: Unverified Mock Interactions

```java
// BAD — mocks the repository but never verifies it was called
when(repo.save(any())).thenReturn(savedEntity);
var result = service.create(input);
assertEquals("id-1", result.getId());
// ... no verify(repo).save(...)

// GOOD
verify(repo).save(captor.capture());
assertEquals(input.getName(), captor.getValue().getName());
```

**Why forbidden:** If the code under test *stops* calling the repository (bug),
the test still passes because `assertEquals` only checks the return value that
was stubbed. Always `verify` critical interactions.

---

## AP-07: Over-mocking (Mocking the Class Under Test)

```java
// BAD — mocking methods on the class you're testing
var service = spy(new OrderService(repo));
doReturn(discount).when(service).calculateDiscount(any());

// GOOD — mock only dependencies, test the class directly
var service = new OrderService(mockRepo);
var result = service.processOrder(order);
```

**Why forbidden:** Spying on the class under test makes the test fragile and
couples it to internal method structure. If `calculateDiscount` is refactored
inline, the test breaks even though behaviour is unchanged.

**Exception:** `@Spy` on the class under test is acceptable *only* when testing a
template-method pattern where the overridden method is the explicit contract.

---

## AP-08: Testing Impossible Paths

```java
// BAD — constructor-injected dependency can never be null at runtime
@Test
void process_nullRepository_throwsNPE() {
    var service = new FooService(null);
    assertThrows(NullPointerException.class, () -> service.find("x"));
}
```

**Why forbidden:** Spring's constructor injection guarantees dependencies are
non-null. Testing null-injection scenarios adds noise with zero production
coverage.

---

## AP-09: Ignoring Return Values in Verify

```java
// BAD — verifies the call was made but ignores what was sent
verify(restClient).post(any(), any());

// GOOD — capture and assert the request body
verify(restClient).post(eq(expectedUri), captor.capture());
assertEquals("expected-payload", captor.getValue().getBody());
```

**Why forbidden:** Verifying that a method was called with `any()` matchers only
proves invocation count, not correctness of the data sent. If the code sends
the wrong payload, this test passes.

---

## AP-10: Hardcoded Mocks That Mirror Implementation

```java
// BAD — test mirrors the exact implementation step-by-step
when(step1.run(input)).thenReturn(mid);
when(step2.run(mid)).thenReturn(output);
var result = pipeline.execute(input);
assertEquals(output, result);
// This test will break if the pipeline reorders steps, even if output is the same

// GOOD — focus on input → output contract
var result = pipeline.execute(input);
assertEquals(expectedOutput, result);
verify(step1).run(any());
verify(step2).run(any());
```

**Why forbidden:** Tests that mirror implementation create a 1:1 coupling. Any
refactoring breaks the test even when behaviour is preserved. Focus on the
*contract* (input → output + side effects), not the *choreography*.

---

## AP-11: Missing Error-Path Tests

```java
// BAD — only happy path, no test for when the HTTP call fails
@Test
void fetchUser_returnsUser() {
    when(restClient.get(uri)).thenReturn(userJson);
    var user = service.fetchUser("id-1");
    assertEquals("John", user.getName());
}
// ... no test for 404, 500, timeout, malformed JSON

// GOOD — separate error scenarios
@Test void fetchUser_404_throwsNotFoundException() { ... }
@Test void fetchUser_500_throwsServiceException() { ... }
@Test void fetchUser_malformedJson_throwsParseException() { ... }
```

**Why forbidden:** Production bugs most often live in error paths. Skipping them
means the highest-risk code is the least tested.

---

## AP-12: Asserting on `toString()` Instead of Fields

```java
// BAD
assertEquals("User{name=John, age=30}", result.toString());

// GOOD
assertEquals("John", result.getName());
assertEquals(30, result.getAge());
```

**Why forbidden:** `toString()` is a debug aid, not a contract. Any formatting
change breaks the test without a real bug. Assert on actual fields.
